response.translation: Is this, then, anything other than the menstrual blood [236] and the seed? I for my part know of no third thing; but since the substance of the body in those that are generated comes from these principles, the strictly first constitution would be said to consist not for the most part of the bodies mentioned, but of them alone. And yet why do I say 'the strictly first'? For if we recall what sort of thing Hippocrates described the six-day seed to be, we shall know clearly that the innate body still persists in it. For before any nature of bone or vein or artery or nerve or cartilage or ligament appears in the embryo, the only thing that exists in them is the innate hot body.

For a certain unformed soft flesh, resembling a clot of blood, takes over the first appearance of the embryo, having within it certain things, as Hippocrates named them, like blood-weals, from the substance of the seed, the whiteness in it being present; and later, from the great alteration that comes about continuously, a kind of outline of bone and cartilage and ligament and nerve and artery and vein is brought to completion, at which time the innate hot body [237] is still remaining in those that are being carried in the womb, but it is always greatest, and the more so, in proportion as the things carried in the womb grow. The innate hot body of them, which was blood and seed, becomes less; while a variety of acquired bodies is added. For none of the things mentioned is innate in animals, but all are acquired; and if indeed an animal could ever become wholly bony or sinewy, the innate heat would in that way be destroyed. But this is impossible, whereas it is possible for the substance of the bones and cartilages and ligaments and nerves and arteries to prevail. At any rate those of the animals that have reached extreme old age, having the least of the bloody nature, are composed, almost entirely, of bones alone and nerves, of membranes and ligaments, of arteries and veins and cartilages. For of all the parts of the animal the flesh alone is bloody, and of this the aged have the least, and this little-blooded and hard. And of the other parts mentioned none is bloody.
uncertain_greek: πλεῖστον ἀεί τε καὶ μᾶλλόν ἐστιν

response.translation: One must not, therefore, measure simply by the bulk of the substance the quantity of the connate body, which, after the most active [238] of the qualities in it, has been named the innate heat; rather one must consider the proportion by comparing it with the bodies that are not innate. For just as in the bath-house we say that there is much vapour or, by Zeus, smoke or some other such thing, not referring simply to the size of the buildings but to the air proper to the bath-house, so too in the case of man we shall say that the substance of the innate heat is either very great or small by comparing it with the bodies that are not innate. For the infant has everything most bloody, to the point that something of this kind appears even in the bones. Conversely, the old have everything most bloodless, right down to the flesh; for even in this there is the least blood. But if the blood is the innate hot body, it would follow, then, from these considerations that the innate hot body is greatest in those who are growing and least in those who have grown old.

So too the seed, composed of the serous moisture and of the pneuma that is in it, is least in those who have grown old and greatest in the bodies of those who are growing, and among these especially [239] in the youngest, as we demonstrated in the commentaries On Seed. If, at any rate, you will raise the difficulty whether the body of those who are growing is easily consumed and flows away: well, in the case of other things, at least, you are not unaware that hot water or oil or any of the fluids of this kind is wholly dispersed in the shortest time, whereas neither earth nor stone nor any other of the things cold and dry by nature is. For in all things that exist there are two qualities most suited for dispersal, moisture and heat, and conversely two for permanence, dryness and coldness; so that it is no wonder if the bodies of children, on account of their moisture and heat, are easily transpired, while those of the old are not easily so, since they have a substance congealed by dryness and cooling. So that, my excellent Lycus, you bring charges concerning the very things for which you ought to have been censured. You have shown yourself, then, to be ignorant of one of the first lessons, which none of those who have been properly introduced is ignorant of.

For the bulk of the body judges a simple substance to be abundant, but one that is composite from differing [240] constituents is judged so by the proportion of the things mixed, just as in the case of the brain or any of the other parts. Thus at any rate those who mix wine with water for drinking say either that the wine is more or the water, or neither, when they have arrived at a well-measured blend. And no one is so senseless that, having thrown a cotyle of water into a jar of wine, he says that the water in the jar is more than that in a small cup, when, as it happens, there are three cyathi in the latter, of which one is of water and two of wine. But Lycus, I suppose, will deny that even the preparation called the tetrapharmakon, composed of wax and fat and pitch and resin, all put together in equal amounts, has more pitch if someone puts in double the amount of the others; rather here too he will say that one should examine whether it is a whole jar that is full of the tetrapharmakon preparation or some small little dish, and then he will say that the jar has far more pitch than the little dish, even if the former was made from equal amounts of the four, while in the little dish the pitch is double the others.

If, then, all such errors [241] belong to those others who are unable to distinguish the 'much' according to proportion and mixture from what is so called simply according to the common measure, it is not in the same manner as that in which Lycus brought his charge against Hippocrates; for the substance of the innate heat is greatest in those who are growing, relative to the proportion of the others, and the quality that accompanies it likewise, since the proper qualities are inseparable from their substances, just as indeed the powers also are. Thus at any rate even if you throw into the tetrapharmakon pitch in excess of the proportion of the others, you will say that not only its substance but also its quality and its power show themselves greater, and for this reason also that the moisture, whatever belongs to the pitch, has been increased. It is clear, then, that according to the three significations of 'much' that have been written by Lycus, both the pitch will be said to be more in the tetrapharmakon and the innate heat in animals.
uncertain_greek: ὥσπερ γε τῷ καὶ αἱ δυνάμεις
τὸ ὑγρὸν ὅπερ ἂν τῆς πίττης ηὐξῆσθαι

response.translation: Still more, in the case of things in which the ingredients mixed have not been blended whole through the whole of one another, it is quite evident that according to the three modes which Lycus stated one thing is said to be more than another, as in the case of [242] this drug, which is among the most customary, and which is composed of iris and aristolochia and the flour of bitter vetch and frankincense, all equal to one another in weight: one could make one of them double and mix it with the others kept equal, for instance, as it might be, the aristolochia. It is true, then, to say with regard to their mixture that the aristolochia is more in substance and in quality and in activity, and prevails over the others. One might say this very same thing also in the case of the bath-house, when it has within it not only the well-tempered air but has taken on in addition something of smoke and of vapour. For of these, sometimes the smoke can be more, sometimes the vapour, just as also the air of the bath-house that is in accordance with nature. But we say 'simply' not of what is more by the excess of its substance, with which it is necessary that the quality and the activity deriving from it also increase together. Let it be supposed, at any rate, that the substance of the smoke is more than that of the other two; you will then rightly say that the quality of the smoke too is more than the quality of the others, and the activity as well.
uncertain_greek: τὸ δ’ ἁπλῶς οὐ τῷ πλείονι

response.translation: It is agreed, [243] however, that a quality does not become 'more' than a quality, but 'more intense', just as also 'fainter', not 'less', though such a use of the words is extremely common throughout the whole book and in all the arts. And why need one mention the others, when we have a manifest witness to the argument in the fevers themselves, which everyone says every day have become greater or less than one another, and at times that someone is feverish less or more, and that this man's fever is the same yesterday or today? With it thus laid down that the 'more' in respect of quality is so spoken of, it is no wonder, in a bath-house in which the substance of smoke is greater, to say that the quality too has become more, and the activity: 'strong' and 'more intense', if we are naming properly; 'greater' and 'more', if by misuse. For the smoke will evidently bite the eyes to the degree that it increases also in substance; so that, since the qualities proper to the substances and the activities always increase together with the substances, one might truly say that in such a bath-house the smoke is greatest.
uncertain_greek: τὸν δὲ τοῦδε κατὰ τὸν αὐτὸν χθὲς ἢ σήμερον

response.translation: But let it be supposed again, as we were saying, [244] that there is something of vapour and of smoke in the bath-house, while the substance proper to the air both is and becomes greatest in proportion, like that of the heat innate in animals; for it will be said now too that in the bath-house the proper heat is greatest. Does it, then, fall at all short of this, that the humours in the animal too, from whose exhalation comes the heat that strikes those who touch it from outside? For one heat is kindled from the blood, another from the phlegm, another from the yellow or the black bile. In the case of children, then, the substance of the blood is greatest according to the proportion of the mixture (for of this one must always remind, as if they were held fast by lethargy, those who talk such nonsense as Lycus wrote), and so is the quality that increases together with it, being wholesome and friendly, not distressing and biting to those who touch, and the activity, according to which the digestions become neither nidorous nor acid, as in the case of phlegm.

In every mode, then, most noble Lycus, the innate heat is more in those who are growing, so that Hippocrates erred in nothing, [245] but rather you have been convicted of malicious attack. For you have shown, from what you wrote, that you have not been introduced at all by teachers so as to understand anything of the Hippocratic doctrines, and that you openly bring charges against things of which you have no knowledge at all; and you have been caught making a most ignorant refutation, attempting through it to overturn the constitution of every art, while, being ignorant of what Plato wrote about these matters, you often contradict yourself, corrupting the young, all those who, like you, being unexercised in logical theory, do not know how to distinguish true arguments from false. On top of all this you have shown yourself at once most audacious and a babbler, having undertaken to write exegeses of what was said by Hippocrates without having first learned it.
